title: Coroner's inquest into shooting turns testy
subtitle: HOUSTON, B.C. - The coroner's inquest into the shooting of millworker Ian Bush by an RCMP officer became testy Tuesday as Coroner Shane DeMeyer ruled questions about the police investigation into the killinginappropriate.
article: HOUSTON, B.C. - The coroner's inquest into the shooting of millworker Ian Bush by a RCMP officer became testy today as coroner Shane DeMeyer ruled inappropriate questions about the shoddy police investigation into the killing. In a startling move, DeMeyer said "critiquiing or commenting" on the investigation by the RCMP goes "beyond the scope" of the inquest and should be dealt with in another forum such as a public inquiry. He said he would stop questions related to the Mountie's handling of the slaying that occurred in the local RCMP detachment Oct. 29, 2005. The family was shocked and through their lawyer Howard Rubin said they believed it important for the five person coroner's jury to hear how police responded. "There have been several in-custody deaths and no police officer has been prosecuted in the last few years," Rubin complained. "If police knew there would be a real investigation that would stand as a warning to them that they are being watched." His pleas fell on deaf ears. "I am mindful that there is a legitimate ongoing public policy debate as to how deaths in police custory are investigated," DeMeyer said. "In my view, the debate centers on the question of whether an independent body is better suited to carry out such investigations than a group from the police force itself. In my view, a coroner's inquest is not the proper forum for examining that public policy issues for the following reasons: "1. in my view, it is unlikely that deaths in police custody will be prevented or lessened in response to a change in the manner in which they are investigated; "2. the discussion of that public policy debate involves consideration of matters much broader than the inquest mandate; eg. how is such an agency to be constituted and funded; what powers would such an agency require; are there negative implications for investigations undertaken in such a manner; "3. broader public policy debates are better suited to the public inquiry process so all interested parties and stakeholders can be heard; in this matter the jury is directed to focus on the circumstances leading to the death of Mr. Bush and making recommendations to prevent or lessen the likelihood of such a death." Bush was shot in the back of the head after being arrested for giving police a false name when questioned about having an open bottle of beer outside a hockey game. Const. Paul Koester said he shot Bush after the man sucker punched him and began choking the life out of him. The rookie officer, who was 28 and had been on the beat for only five months, said Bush was on top of his back and he was face down on a couch when he fired his service pistol. But the family and others have cast doubt on that version of events in part because Koester refuses to re-enact what happened and at least one expert says the physical evidence does not support his rendition. There were also questions raised about the autopsy and the pathologist's report - in particular his failure to mention a large bruise on Bush's thigh and his testimony that it was not a bruise but an in-grown hair. In his ruling today, the coroner said he would not call celebrated forensic pathologist Dr. John Butt as recommended by the family to correct the medical record. Instead, he said he had commissioned his own report from a third pathologist, Dr. Richard Crawford, who agreed with the family that the mark was a bruise from a blunt trauma injury consistent with being kneed in the groin. His report was entered as evidence but he will not be called to testify. The Bush family wants the inquest jury to recommend that the Mounties not investigate themselves in cases involving police shootings because of the appearance of bias. Rubin appeared extremely frustrated by the coroner's order that such lines of inquiry were going to be. "I believe the RCMP handled Const. Koester with kid gloves and didn't press him to provide a reconstruction (of the killing) or a statement," he said. Within an hour of the shooting, a call had been placed to a lawyer on Koester's behalf and he was then allowed to give advice to the police officer. Koester did not provide a written statement for three weeks after the shooting, and then he did so with the help of a lawyer and his wife. He didn't do a face-to-face interview with investigators for more than three months. By comparison, detectives interviewed Bush's friends the day following the shooting wtihin minutes of telling them he was dead. But DeMayeyer was implacable - not only did he warn Rubin that his questions would be censored if they weren't on point, but he also demanded the family's blood-splatter expert edit out portions of his report concerning his recreation of the slaying before testifying Thursday. Const. Joseph Slemko, of Edmonton police, provided a report to the family that says the forensic evidence does not support Koester's account of what happened. DeMeyer said he will allow only a portion of Slemko's findings into evidence because he is qualified as an expert solely on blood-splatters. For instance, Slemko told Rubin in an e-mail that the investigation by the RCMP in this case was so sloppy it made him "physically ill." In the aftermath of the coroner's order, tensions between the lawyers involved in the inquest rose and at one point coroner's counsel Mitch Houg yelled across the room at Rubin telling him not to approach the DeMeyer unless invited. "I don't think I should be lectured by counsel," Rubin replied testily. Later, the coroner had to tell RCMP lawyer Helen Roberts to be more respectful in her questioning after she asked whether one witness was "lying" and described Bush's behaviour the night he was killed as "stupid." Roberts, who bristled at every suggestion the force screwed up, said the public should realize the Mounties will conduct an official complaint investigation in this case. "The RCMP is not trying to avoid a review of their investigation," she said. "This is not a proper forum for that." No, this appears to be little more than a forum for endorsing the police version of events. As I said Tuesday, a whitewash. imulgrew@png.canwest.com
